headline: New law creates heart-condition education efforts and grants to put CPR training and defibrillators in public schools.
what_it_does: The law requires the Department of Health and Human Services to share information about cardiomyopathy, a group of heart muscle conditions, and about using automated external defibrillators (AEDs) with school staff, families, and others. It also requires HHS to create tools to help assess a person's risk of cardiomyopathy. The CDC and the National Institutes of Health must report on their research and tracking of the condition. It also sets up a grant program to pay for CPR training and AEDs in public schools.

who_it_affects.how: Schools can apply for federal grants to provide CPR training and buy AEDs.

who_it_affects.group: Teachers, coaches, and other school professionals
who_it_affects.how: They will receive federal information about cardiomyopathy and how to use AEDs, and some may get CPR training.
Families will get information about cardiomyopathy, and students may attend schools better equipped to respond to heart emergencies.

who_it_affects.group: People with or at risk of cardiomyopathy
who_it_affects.how: Federal agencies will develop risk assessment tools and report on research related to the condition.
They must share information, create risk tools, and submit reports on cardiomyopathy research and tracking.

when_it_takes_effect: Enacted December 23, 2024; specific deadlines for programs and reports are not stated in the summary.
